doc.title: Victor Rendon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Jelly Roll Morton's Spanish tinge
summary: The Latin tinge, the cinquillo rhythm, Mexican teachers in New Orleans, and Gottschalk.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: This is sort of a historical question, I don’t know if you’ll have an opinion on it. Jelly Roll Morton, you know the early jazz pianist, was quoted when people would say well what is jazz, and he would say it’s this and that, but it has to have a Spanish tinge to it. And I always wondered what he meant by that. I wonder if you have an opinion on it. To me when he says “Spanish” I think he means the music comes from south of our border.
There was a lot of, I’m sure you have that book, “The Latin Tinge” who was the author of that? I don’t remember but you know what I’m talking about.

And it talks a lot about the Caribbean influence. [scats] It has like what they called that cincio rhythm [scats] you could put it in clave. A lot of it has the [scats] that’s the cincio. [scat] It’s five notes. Cincio means cinco and that music came to New Orleans. And a lot of it came via Mexico, I didn’t know that, that there was like a family of teachers that came through New Orleans to teach and they were very influential in the early development of jazz, which I never knew. So I think that might be what he was referring to, I can not be one hundred percent, but that Latino tinge, what this author referred to, that’s what he was talking about. There was a guy named Gottschalk.

And he was influenced by that, or he actually went to South America and died or something, if I’m correct. He got sick, but it was that [scats] that type of thing that’s prevalent in the early jazz stages. That’s my opinion from what I’ve read and listened to over the years.
